title: Pilot weekly thresholds vs baseline sync — CascadeHealth
summary: Weekly POC sync to compare Redwood pilot latency/throughput against the customer's baseline provider. Reviewed p50/p95/p99 numbers, cold vs warm starts, batching effects, and fallback behavior. Agreed on follow-up stress tests and a final short sweep with the product team before the pilot wrap-up.
topics: Throughput and batching tuning (batch size, inter-batch delay)
Cold-start vs warm-cache behavior and KV cache tuning
Next steps: stress tests, security docs, pricing recap
next_steps: Priya to run 4k-token tail-latency stress run and upload CSV by 2025-10-03
Jordan to send pricing delta sheet and dedicated vs hosted comparison by 2025-10-02
Tom to share internal traffic profile and peak window logs by 2025-10-04
Schedule final demo with product on 2025-10-08 (Sara to confirm)
action_items: Priya Patel (SE) — run 4k token p99 stress test (include cold/warm) — 2025-10-03
Jordan Meyers (AE) — send pricing delta sheet + single-page SLA comparison — 2025-10-02

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-30 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Meyers (Redwood AE); Priya Patel (Redwood SE); Dr. Elena Ruiz (CascadeHealth, Head of ML); Tom Briggs (Infra Lead); Sara Kim (Product Owner)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick note, I recorded this for the POC notes, hope that's okay.
[00:10] Dr. Elena: Yeah that's fine. We're mostly here for the numbers and the tuning advice.
[00:18] Priya: Great. I pulled the bench sheet — I'll share my screen — I have the baseline provider numbers (what you sent last week) side-by-side with our pilot run metrics. Quick caveat: some transcriptions in the auto sheets swapped KV cache for KV cash in one column, so ignore that label.
[00:38] Tom: Haha yep we saw that. The baseline p99 we had was about 420 ms for 512 tokens, with throughput topping at ~25 rps on average.
[00:48] Priya: Right, and in our dedicated pilot pool the p99 for the same profile was 180 ms and throughput steady at 65–70 rps. Those are after enabling continuous batching and the lightweight quantization profile.
[01:05] Dr. Elena: That's a pretty big delta. Can you walk through what triggers that p99 reduction — is it batching, or different kernels?
[01:14] Priya: It's a mix. We use a kernel selection path tuned for your sequence length distribution — so for many short prompts we use vectorized attentions that shave per-token time. Then continuous batching helps fill the GPU more efficiently without increasing observed latency for p50. The KV cache behavior also reduces repeated prefix work, but there's two caveats: cold starts and long-token requests (4k+).
[01:40] Jordan: Also important — our routing had a small percentage of fallback to a cheaper variant during one burst window we saw yesterday, which we fixed; that showed up as a few outlier 800 ms calls in the logs.
[01:50] Tom: Those outliers are the thing I worry about. Our SLO target is 250 ms p99 during business-hours. How reliable is your p99 under load?
[02:01] Priya: In our stress run the p99 stayed under 220 ms for sustained 60 rps for 30 minutes when using dedicated. Under hosted (shared) it was closer to 300–350 ms at the same qps; so dedicated is the safer lane if your SLO is 250 ms.
[02:20] Dr. Elena: How about cold-start behavior? We have intermittent burst traffic from some batch pipelines.
[02:27] Priya: Cold-starts depend on whether the model worker has a warm KV cache and whether it was recently used. For your shape we saw cold p99 up to 1.1–1.3 s on first requests in an idle pool. Warmed workers drop back to the numbers I mentioned. We recommend a small keep-alive or scheduled ping during your batch windows.
[02:47] Tom: Could the keep-alive strategy add cost? We run a lot of short, low-importance checks.
[02:53] Jordan: Yes, small cost tradeoff — but often cheaper than paying tail-latency penalties or user complaints. Redwood Optimize has a suggested keep-alive window and a cost delta estimate we can share.
[03:05] Sara: Can we talk about throughput scaling — in your runs you said 65–70 rps. Our baseline scaled up to 80 rps but with p99 at 420ms. There seems to be a tradeoff.
[03:17] Priya: Exactly. There's a curve: you can get higher rps by increasing batch size and letting more in-flight requests join a batch. That increases p50 slightly but if the model/provisioning is right, p99 can remain acceptable. For Cascade's traffic profile we suggest an adaptive batching policy: keep small batches during interactive windows, switch to larger batching during peak background processing.
[03:40] Tom: How does fallback work? We had some incidents where a burst hit a capacity throttle and requests got queued or fell back to a smaller model which produced lower quality.
[03:49] Priya: We have fallback policies configurable: hard throttle (reject), queue until capacity frees, or degrade to a compatible lower-size model. For the pilot we had an automatic degrade to a quantized variant which saved cost but degraded tail latency for some edge cases; we flipped that to automatic fallback off for your test cluster.
[04:10] Dr. Elena: Any notes on output quality delta when you quantize? We ran a simple eval and saw small regressions in answer length and extra hallucinations in 1–2% of the prompts.
[04:22] Priya: That's expected; the quantization profile we used is mild (int8-ish) but we can provide a report with pass/fail on your eval set and toggle to a higher-precision profile if the quality regression is unacceptable.
[04:35] Jordan: Quick interjection — I know pricing matters. For the same sustained load, dedicated committed nodes are about 30–40% cheaper at the per-token level compared to on-demand hosted at high qps, but there's a commit/contract implication. I'll send a single-page price delta after this call.
[04:52] Tom: That helps. Also want to call out the security checklist — we had a quick internal review and they asked if Redwood logs include token-level content in audit logs.
[05:03] Priya: Short answer: we offer configurable audit logging. You can redact request/response content and keep metadata-only logs; we can share the SOC2/ISO docs and the KMS integration notes. Jordan will follow up with the redacted examples.
[05:18] Dr. Elena: Great. Back to measurements — can you share the raw CSVs of the runs? We want to plug them into our incident simulation tool.
[05:26] Priya: Yep, I'll upload the bench CSVs for yesterday's sustained 60 rps run and the 30-minute stress window. Expect two files: bench_20250929_sustained_60.csv and ColdWarmSweep_20250929.csv.
[05:36] Tom: When you say "sustained 60 rps" how many worker slots was that? We need equivalent VM/GPU counts to compare.
[05:42] Priya: That was 4 V100-equivalent slots in the Dedicated pool; batch size averaged 8 for that workload. I'll annotate the CSV with the worker counts.
[05:51] Dr. Elena: There's also the matter of our 4k token path — we saw higher variance.
[05:58] Priya: For long contexts we saw p99 around 650–700 ms even on dedicated in that run; that's mostly memory-bound and kernel selection is less efficient for long seqs. We can test a long-token specialized kernel and report back.
[06:12] Jordan: Action item: Priya will run a dedicated 4k-tail stress with warm/warm+cache priming and give p50/p95/p99 + distribution by 2025-10-03.
[06:21] Dr. Elena: Sounds good. Also can you re-run one of the tests with our actual traffic pattern? Not synthetic uniform — we have spiky bursts every hour.
[06:31] Priya: Yes, if you share the traffic trace Tom mentioned we can replay it.
[06:35] Tom: I'll upload the trace to the secure folder by Friday.
[06:38] Jordan: Let's touch briefly on throttling behavior in degraded region — we configured automatic fallback off in the pilot cluster but in production we usually prefer graceful queueing for a short window before rejecting. Thoughts?
[06:49] Dr. Elena: Queueing seems safer if we want to protect quality. But we need a bounded maximum queue time.
[06:55] Priya: Agree — we can set a hard queue timeout of X ms and a priority threshold so internal batch jobs don't stomp interactive traffic. We can model this in the next run.
[07:08] Sara: Is there anything we need to change in the client SDK to support adaptive batching or priority tags?
[07:14] Priya: Minimal change — a header for priority and a small SDK flag. We'll put a sample patch in the repo.
[07:20] Jordan: Okay near the 40-minute mark here, let's go through the recorded numbers: baseline p99 420 ms, baseline throughput 25 rps; Redwood dedicated p99 180 ms, throughput 65–70 rps; Redwood hosted p99 ~300–350 ms at same qps. Cold start p99 up to 1.2 s. Long-token (4k) p99 ~650–700 ms on dedicated current kernels.
[07:45] Dr. Elena: That summary looks right. For our acceptance we'll need sustained p99 < 250 ms and less than 1.5% of requests > 1s across typical interactive windows.
[07:58] Jordan: Noted. That matches the action item for the 4k run and the replay of production trace.
[08:06] Tom: Anything on error modes — e.g., OOM or retries — in your logs from the pilot?
[08:11] Priya: We saw one OOM in a misconfigured quantized variant which caused a retry loop; fixed by adjusting the memlimit and disabling that variant for the cluster. We'll run another stability sweep.
[08:23] Dr. Elena: Can we get the stability sweep results before we commit to Dedicated? We want evidence beyond performance — also reliability under noisy neighbors.
[08:32] Jordan: Yes, we can run a 48-hour soak test in a semi-dedicated environment and share the summary. That would include error rates, restarts, and any falls-backs observed.
[08:42] Priya: We'll correlate with request IDs so you can surface incidents.
[08:46] Sara: Final question — if we sign for dedicated reserved capacity, what's the minimum term?
[08:52] Jordan: Typical is a 3-month minimum for pilot-level reserved pools, but for production we do 12-month commits with volume discounts. I'll include both options in the price delta.
[09:03] Dr. Elena: Okay let's close with next steps.
[09:08] Jordan: Recap: Priya runs the 4k-tail test and a replay with your trace (Tom); uploads CSVs; Jordan sends pricing and SOC2/security redaction examples; Tom uploads traffic trace; schedule final product sweep on 2025-10-08 pending Sara.
[09:24] Tom: I'll get the trace in by Friday.
[09:27] Sara: I'll try to confirm the 10/08 meeting later today.
[09:31] Dr. Elena: Thanks everyone, this was useful.
[09:33] Jordan: Thanks all — we'll follow up in Slack and drop files in the shared folder.
[09:36] (call ends)
